claim: BEST4 overexpression halved cell proliferating rates of HCT116 and Caco2 CRC cell lines compared to empty vector controls.
source: BEST4 overexpression halved cell proliferating rates of their respective empty vector (EV) controls when they were monitored in live and analysed using InCucyte (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by live cell monitoring data using IncuCyte shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: BEST4 overexpression decreased cell viability in HCT116 and Caco2 cells.
source: This was accompanied by decreased cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Knockout of BEST4 in HCT-15 resulted in a 50% increase in proliferation rates compared to parental control.
source: Consequently, there was a 50% increase in proliferation rates and viability compared with the parental control (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and viability data from BEST4 knockout cells shown in Figure 1C, D and supplement

claim: Rescued expression of BEST4 reversed the proliferation effects in BEST4 knockout HCT-15 cells.
source: Rescued expression of BEST4 was able to reverse the observed effects on HCT-15 (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1D and supplement

claim: BEST4 overexpression decreased colony formations by 60% in HCT116 and 70% in Caco2 compared to controls.
source: In contrast to the controls, BEST4 overexpression decreased colony formations of HCT116 and Caco2 by 60% and 70%, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1E

claim: BEST4 deletion increased the number of colonies by fivefold in HCT-15.
source: While BEST4 deletion increased the number of colonies by fivefold in HCT-15 (Figure 1F), the rescued expression counteracted its enhancement (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data from BEST4 knockout cells shown in Figure 1F

claim: Overexpression of BEST4 in HCT116 inhibited transwell migration by 70% and invasion by 80% compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of BEST4 in HCT116 inhibited transwell migration and invasion by 70% and 80%, respectively, compared to EV controls (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration and invasion assay data shown in Figure 1G

claim: BEST4 ablation in HCT-15 increased cell migration by twofold and invasion by threefold.
source: But BEST4 ablation in HCT-15 increased cell migration and invasion by twofold and threefold, respectively.
evidence: Supported by transwell migration and invasion assay data from BEST4 knockout cells

claim: BEST4 expression upregulated CDH1 and TJP1 and downregulated VIM and TWIST1 in HCT116 compared to control.
source: Because EMT initiation is a critical process in tumour progression (Acloque et al., 2009), we evaluated the effect of BEST4 on EMT using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and found that BEST4 expression upregulated CDH1 and TJP1 and downregulated VIM and TWIST1 in HCT116 compared with the control (p<0.05) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and cited reference on EMT

claim: Knockout of BEST4 in HCT15 downregulated CDH1 and TJP1 and upregulated VIM and TWIST1.
source: Conversely, knockout of BEST4 in HCT15 downregulated CDH1 and TJP1 and upregulated VIM and TWIST1.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from BEST4 knockout cells

claim: Rescued expression of BEST4 in HCT-15 reversed the gene alterations caused by BEST4 knockout.
source: Rescued expression of BEST4 in HCT-15 reversed these gene alterations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: Changes in EMT-related genes were consistent with their corresponding protein expression.
source: Changes of these genes were consistent with their corresponding protein expression as analysed by immunoblotting (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C, D and supplement

claim: The sizes and weights of tumours in BEST4 overexpression group were only half of the empty vector control in xenograft mice.
source: Essentially, the sizes and weights of tumours in BEST4 overexpression group were only half of the EV control (Figure 2E and F), in conjunction with the similar magnitude reduction of Ki67+ cells as analysed by immunohistochemistry (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by tumor size, weight, and Ki67 staining data from xenograft experiments shown in Figure 2E-H

claim: BEST4 deterred EMT in xenograft tumors by upregulating E-cadherin and downregulating VIM and TWIST1.
source: Further analysis of the HCT116 tumour tissue lysates showed that BEST4 deterred EMT by upregulating E-cadherin, and downregulating VIM and TWIST1 (Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of tumor tissue lysates shown in Figure 2I and supplement

claim: There were twofold greater liver metastatic nodules in BEST4 deficient tumours than the control in intrasplenic injection model.
source: We observed that there were twofold greater of the liver metastatic nodules in the BEST4 deficient tumours than the control (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: Supported by liver metastasis data from intrasplenic injection model shown in Figure 2J-L

claim: Reconstituted BEST4 expression had no visible metastatic nodules in the liver in the intrasplenic injection model.
source: Conversely, the reconstituted BEST4 expression had no visible metastatic nodules in the liver, and the pathological analysis of the tissue sections by H&E staining also confirmed no detectable metastatic loci in the tissue sections (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: Supported by liver metastasis data and H&E staining from rescue experiments shown in Figure 2J-L

claim: Transfecting Flag-HES4 plasmid DNA into HCT116 resulted in responsive upregulation of both endogenous BEST4 mRNA and protein levels.
source: Upon transfecting the Flag-HES4 plasmid DNA into HCT116, we observed a responsive upregulation of both endogenous BEST4 mRNA and protein levels compared to the control transfectant (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data from HES4 overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3A and supplement

claim: Knocking down endogenous HES4 with shRNAs in LST174 resulted in downregulation of endogenous BEST4.
source: This intrinsic association was further supported by knocking down the endogenous HES4 with two pairs of short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) in LST174 that resulted in downregulation of endogenous BEST4 (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data from HES4 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3B and supplement

claim: HES4 overexpression resulted in a fourfold increase in BEST4 promoter activity compared to empty vector control.
source: Our results showed a fourfold increase in the promoter activity compared to the EV control (Figure 3C), Furthermore, chromatin immunoprecipitation-quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR) analysis using a Flag antibody to IP for HES4 revealed a 12-fold enrichment of the P3 region upstream of the BEST4 transcriptional start site compared to the control (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by dual-luciferase assay and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: ChIP-qPCR analysis revealed a 12-fold enrichment of the P3 region upstream of the BEST4 transcriptional start site by HES4.
source: Furthermore, chromatin immunoprecipitation-quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR) analysis using a Flag antibody to IP for HES4 revealed a 12-fold enrichment of the P3 region upstream of the BEST4 transcriptional start site compared to the control (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: BEST4 overexpression in HCT116 cells did not affect HES4 mRNA expression.
source: Interestingly, BEST4 overexpression in HCT116 cells did not affect HES4 mRNA expression as quantified by qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that HES4 regulates BEST4 expression upstream.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: HES4 regulates BEST4 expression upstream.
source: Interestingly, BEST4 overexpression in HCT116 cells did not affect HES4 mRNA expression as quantified by qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that HES4 regulates BEST4 expression upstream.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BEST4 does not affect HES4 expression, supported by qPCR data

claim: Nuclear colocalisation of BEST4 and HES4 was observed in HCT116 cells co-transfected with BEST4-HA and Flag-HES4 plasmid DNAs.
source: This speculation is supported by immunofluorescence staining, where we observed nuclear colocalisation of BEST4 (green) and HES4 (red) in HCT116 cells co-transfected with BEST4-HA and Flag-HES4 plasmid DNAs, along with additional cytoplasmic expression of BEST4 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3E

claim: BEST4 and HES4 were reciprocally copurified from nuclear protein lysates in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: By conducting IP with antibodies specific to Flag or HA, we showed that BEST4 and HES4 were reciprocally copurified from the nuclear protein lysates, but not with IgG controls (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Flag-HES4 or BEST4-HA transfectants significantly decreased TWIST1 promoter activity by almost half compared to empty vector control.
source: In comparison with the EV control, Flag-HES4 or BEST4-HA transfectants significantly decreased TWIST1 promoter activity by almost half, as evaluated by the dual-luciferase assay (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by dual-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A

claim: BEST4 transfectant enhanced inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter by 70% in HES4-expressing HCT116.
source: Essentially, the BEST4 transfectant enhanced inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter by 70% in HES4-expressing HCT116 (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), hence suggesting that BEST4 mediates the inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter activity by HES4.
evidence: Supported by dual-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B and supplement

claim: BEST4 mediates the inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter activity by HES4.
source: Essentially, the BEST4 transfectant enhanced inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter by 70% in HES4-expressing HCT116 (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), hence suggesting that BEST4 mediates the inhibition of the TWIST1 promoter activity by HES4.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BEST4 enhances HES4's inhibition of TWIST1 promoter, supported by dual-luciferase assay data

claim: BEST4 and TWIST1 were copurified from nuclear protein lysates in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) with antibodies to Myc or HA showed that they were copurified from the nuclear protein lysates, but not with the IgG controls from the transfectant cell lysates (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D and supplement

claim: Knockdown of endogenous BEST4 in HES4-expressing HCT116 cells substantially decreased Flag-HES4 coprecipitation with TWIST1.
source: Additionally, the knockdown of endogenous BEST4 in HES4-expressing HCT116 cells substantially decreased Flag-HES4 coprecipitation from the nuclear protein lysates, while Myc-TWIST1 expression remained constant, as determined by co-IP with antibodies to Flag or My (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E and supplement

claim: HES4 overexpression in HCT116 cells resulted in upregulation of TJP1 and E-cadherin epithelial molecules and downregulation of TWIST1 protein.
source: Our results showed there were upregulation of TJP1 and E-cadherin epithelial molecules, and downregulation of TWIST1 protein (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and the VIM mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 4F and supplements

claim: Knocking down endogenous HES4 in LS174T cells caused downregulation of epithelial markers and upregulation of mesenchymal markers.
source: Nevertheless, knocking down endogenous HES4 in LS174T cells using shRNAs targeting two HES4 domains caused the opposite effect (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from HES4 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4G and supplement

claim: Knocking down endogenous BEST4 in HES4-expressing HCT116 resulted in downregulation of E-cadherin and TJP1, with upregulation of TWIST1 protein and VIM mRNA.
source: To determine if BEST4 is downstream signal that relays HES4 to regulate TWIST1 expression and consequently EMT induction, we knocked down endogenous BEST4 with RNAs silencing (siRNAs) in HES4-expressing HCT116 and showed the corresponding downregulation of E-cadherin and TJP1, with upregulation of TWIST1 protein and the VIM mRNA, as analysed by immunoblotting and qPCR (Figure 4H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and D).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data from BEST4 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4H and supplements

claim: Inhibition of EMT induction by HES4 is BEST4-mediated by downregulation of TWIST1 expression in CRC.
source: Hence, inhibition of EMT induction by HES4 is BEST4-mediated by downregulation of TWIST1 expression in CRC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BEST4 knockdown reverses HES4's effects on EMT markers

claim: BEST4 significantly increased chloride/calcium fluxes and activated their exchanges in HCT116 cells.
source: After respectively incubating BEST4-expresing HCT116 and the EV control with 300 μM DIDS (a broad blocker of chloride channel), or a gradient increase in doses of CaCCinh-A01 (a specific inhibitor of native CaCCs), or 1 μM ionomycin (a calcium ionophore to activate the chloride channel) as published previously (Liu et al., 2015), we showed that BEST4 significantly increased chloride/calcium fluxes and activated their exchanges and the expected inhibition by DIDS, CaCCinh-A01, or ionomycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by chloride/calcium flux assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and cited reference

claim: BEST4 protein-mediated EMT suppression is independent of its channel function in HCT116.
source: Through immunoblotting analysis, we recapitulated that BEST4 simultaneously upregulated both TJP1 and E-cadherin, and downregulated TWIST1. Essentially, the levels of these proteins remained constantly expressed when the cells were treated with DIDS or CaCCinh-A01 or ionomycin, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F). Hence, these results suggest BEST4 protein-mediated EMT suppression is independent of its channel function in HCT116.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing EMT marker expression is unchanged by channel inhibitors, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: BEST4 was in the top four significantly downregulated genes in CRC compared to adjacent normal tissues in RNA-sequencing analysis.
source: Initially with high-throughput whole transcriptome sequencing analysis of five pairs of CRCs and adjacent normal tissues (ANTs), we identified several significantly downregulated genes in CRC compared to ANTs; BEST4 was in the top four (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: BEST4 was expressed significantly less in adenomas and tumours than in adjacent normal tissues.
source: Further validation by qPCR in the paired tissues of 50 colorectal adenomas and 124 CRC showed that the BEST4 was expressed significantly less in adenomas and tumours than in ANTs (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: BEST4 protein was downregulated in CRC compared to adjacent normal tissues.
source: Immunoblotting analysis of tissue lysates from five paired randomly selected samples showed that BEST4 protein was downregulated in CRC (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from patient samples shown in Figure 5E and supplement

claim: Normal colorectal control tissues consistently expressed higher BEST4 than CRC in TCGA and GTEx datasets.
source: Using public datasets of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx), we measured BEST4 mRNA expression in CRC and matched normal tissues with the online Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis (GEPIA) tool (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/). As shown in Figure 6A the normal colorectal control tissues consistently expressed higher BEST4 than the CRC.
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA and GTEx public datasets shown in Figure 6A

claim: Low BEST4 mRNA expression in males was twice as high as in females.
source: Interestingly, low BEST4 mRNA expression in males was twice as high as in females (p=0.022, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by clinicopathological correlation analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Low BEST4 mRNA expression correlated with more advanced stages of CRC.
source: Accordingly, low BEST4 mRNA expression correlated with more advanced stages (p=0.02, Table 1) and lymph node metastasis (between 0 and 2) (p=0.032, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by clinicopathological correlation analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Low BEST4 mRNA expression correlated with lymph node metastasis.
source: Accordingly, low BEST4 mRNA expression correlated with more advanced stages (p=0.02, Table 1) and lymph node metastasis (between 0 and 2) (p=0.032, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by clinicopathological correlation analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Patients with high BEST4 expression had better overall survival than those with low expression.
source: Patients with high BEST4 expression had better overall survival than those with low expression (p<0.01, Figure 5F), which was confirmed by univariate survival analysis showing a lower risk of death (p<0.001, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5F and univariate analysis in Table 2

claim: Low levels of BEST4 mRNA were associated with poor prognosis of CRC patients in multivariate Cox regression analysis.
source: Multivariate Cox regression analysis indicated that low levels of BEST4 mRNA were associated with poor prognosis of CRC patients (hazard ratio [HR], 0.285; 95% confidence interval, 0.157–0.606; p<0.001; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by multivariate Cox regression analysis shown in Table 2

claim: HES4 mRNA expression was reduced in CRC tissues compared with adjacent normal tissues.
source: After the significant reduction of the HES4 mRNA expression through RNA-sequencing analysis of our CRC patients (Figure 6B and C), we proceeded to investigate the connection between BEST4 and HES4 in TCGA and GTEx (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: There is a positive correlation between BEST4 and HES4 in CRC (R=0.47, p<0.001).
source: Our findings revealed a positive correlation between these genes (R=0.47, p<0.001) (Figure 6D), providing further evidence of their association in CRC.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 6D

claim: There is a positive correlation between BEST4 and CDH1 mRNA (R=0.77, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, we conducted additional mining of TCGA or GTEx datasets using the GEPIA tool (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) and observed a positive correlation between BEST4 and the CDH1 mRNA (R=0.77, p<0.001), with a negative correlation with VIM (R = –0.49, p<0.001) and TWIST1 mRNA (R = –0.39, p<0.001) (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 6E

claim: There is a negative correlation between BEST4 and VIM (R = –0.49, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, we conducted additional mining of TCGA or GTEx datasets using the GEPIA tool (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) and observed a positive correlation between BEST4 and the CDH1 mRNA (R=0.77, p<0.001), with a negative correlation with VIM (R = –0.49, p<0.001) and TWIST1 mRNA (R = –0.39, p<0.001) (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 6F

claim: There is a negative correlation between BEST4 and TWIST1 mRNA (R = –0.39, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, we conducted additional mining of TCGA or GTEx datasets using the GEPIA tool (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) and observed a positive correlation between BEST4 and the CDH1 mRNA (R=0.77, p<0.001), with a negative correlation with VIM (R = –0.49, p<0.001) and TWIST1 mRNA (R = –0.39, p<0.001) (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 6G

claim: BEST4 is a newly identified subtype of the calcium-activated chloride channel family.
source: Bestrophin isoform 4 (BEST4) is a newly identified subtype of the calcium-activated chloride channel family.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing has revealed the existence of a cluster of BEST4+ mature colonocytes in humans.
source: Analysis of colonic epithelial cell diversity by single-cell RNA-sequencing has revealed the existence of a cluster of BEST4+ mature colonocytes in humans.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: BEST4 is co-expressed with HES4 in the nucleus of cells.
source: BEST4 is co-expressed with hairy/enhancer of split 4 (HES4) in the nucleus of cells, and HES4 signals BEST4 by interacting with the upstream region of the BEST4 promoter.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and ChIP data showing nuclear colocalization and promoter binding

claim: HES4 signals BEST4 by interacting with the upstream region of the BEST4 promoter.
source: BEST4 is co-expressed with hairy/enhancer of split 4 (HES4) in the nucleus of cells, and HES4 signals BEST4 by interacting with the upstream region of the BEST4 promoter.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing HES4 binding to BEST4 promoter

claim: BEST4 is epistatic to HES4 and downregulates TWIST1, thereby inhibiting EMT in CRC.
source: BEST4 is epistatic to HES4 and downregulates TWIST1, thereby inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in CRC.
evidence: Supported by promoter activity assays, co-IP experiments, and EMT marker expression data

claim: The low level of BEST4 mRNA is correlated with advanced stage and worse prognosis in CRC.
source: Furthermore, the low level of the BEST4 mRNA is correlated with advanced and the worse prognosis, suggesting its potential role involving CRC progression.
evidence: Supported by clinicopathological correlation and survival analysis data

claim: EMT is a reprogramming process in which epithelial E-cadherin and TJP1 are suppressed, and mesenchymal N-cadherin and VIM are induced.
source: EMT is a reprogramming process in which epithelial E-cadherin and TJP1 are suppressed, and mesenchymal N-cadherin and VIM are induced, transcriptionally mediated by Twist and the Snail family (Dongre and Weinberg, 2019).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Dongre and Weinberg, 2019

claim: Overexpression of TWIST1 significantly enhances the migration and invasion capabilities of CRC cells.
source: Overexpression of TWIST1 significantly enhances the migration and invasion capabilities of CRC cells; furthermore, it is closely associated with metastasis and poor prognosis in patients with CRC (Yusup et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to Yusup et al., 2017 and Zhu et al., 2015

claim: The inhibition of EMT in breast cancer and prostate cancer has been associated with calcium-activated chloride channels.
source: The inhibition of EMT in breast cancer and prostate cancer has been associated with calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) (Porretti et al., 2018; Walia et al., 2012), leading to various evaluations of CaCCs as a potential for cancer therapy (Li et al., 2017; Miotto and Struhl, 2006; Qu et al., 2019; Sui et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies

claim: BEST4 is expressed predominantly in the colon.
source: Although there are four human evolutionarily related genes (BEST1–BEST4) (Miller et al., 2019; Tsunenari et al., 2003), BEST4 is expressed predominantly in the colon (Fagerberg et al., 2014), where it gates electrolyte transportation in human intestinal epithelial cells (Ito et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Fagerberg et al., 2014

claim: BEST4 gates electrolyte transportation in human intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Although there are four human evolutionarily related genes (BEST1–BEST4) (Miller et al., 2019; Tsunenari et al., 2003), BEST4 is expressed predominantly in the colon (Fagerberg et al., 2014), where it gates electrolyte transportation in human intestinal epithelial cells (Ito et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Ito et al., 2013

claim: A group of mature colonocytes expresses BEST4 based on single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis.
source: In a recent analysis based on single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis, it was discovered that a group of mature colonocytes expresses BEST4 (Parikh et al., 2019), and the subset of this group coexists with hairy/enhancer of split 4 positive (HES4+) cells (Parikh et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Parikh et al., 2019

claim: The subset of BEST4+ colonocytes coexists with HES4+ cells.
source: In a recent analysis based on single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis, it was discovered that a group of mature colonocytes expresses BEST4 (Parikh et al., 2019), and the subset of this group coexists with hairy/enhancer of split 4 positive (HES4+) cells (Parikh et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Parikh et al., 2019

claim: HES4 plays a critical role in determining the fate and differentiation of progenitor cells during the development of various organs.
source: HES4 belongs to a family of seven Hes genes (Hes1–7) that encodes a transcription factor with a basic helix-loop-helix motif. It is known to play a critical role in determining the fate and differentiation of progenitor cells during the development of various organs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: HES4 plays an antagonistic role in regulating TWIST1 through protein-protein interaction in bone marrow stromal/stem cell lineage differentiation.
source: The previous study has demonstrated the antagonistic role of HES4 in regulating TWIST1 through protein-protein interaction, which governs the differentiation of bone marrow stromal/stem cell lineage (Cakouros et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Cakouros et al., 2015

claim: Inhibiting the TWIST1 transcriptional factor mediates commitment to the differentiation of human bone marrow stem cells.
source: Inhibiting the TWIST1 transcriptional factor has been shown to mediate commitment to the differentiation of human bone marrow stem cells, as reported by several studies (Cakouros et al., 2015; El Yakoubi et al., 2012; Murato and Hashimoto, 2009; Nichane et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies

claim: This is the first characterisation of the role of BEST4 in suppressing CRC progression and the underlying molecular mechanisms.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first characterisation of the role of BEST4 in suppressing CRC progression and the underlying molecular mechanisms.
evidence: Stated as a claim of novelty by the authors

claim: BEST4 functionally inhibits the development of CRC in vitro and in vivo.
source: In the present study, we demonstrated that BEST4 functionally inhibits the development of CRC in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experimental data presented in the study

claim: BEST4 is transcriptionally regulated and physically interacts with upstream HES4.
source: BEST4 is transcriptionally regulated and physically interacts with upstream HES4, leading to downregulation of TWIST1 and EMT suppression.
evidence: Supported by promoter activity assays, ChIP-qPCR, and co-IP experiments

claim: BEST4-mediated EMT suppression is independent of physiological Ca2+-activated Cl- channels.
source: This suppression is independent of physiological Ca2+-activated Cl- channels since inhibition of BEST4-associated Ca2+- and Cl- fluxes did not alter TJP1/E-cadherin and TWIST1 protein expression.
evidence: Supported by experiments using channel inhibitors showing no effect on EMT marker expression

claim: HES4 is capable of combating EMT induction in a BEST4-dependent manner.
source: While HES1 has been reported to induce EMT and promote metastasis and chemoresistance in CRC (Sun et al., 2017; van Es et al., 2005; Yuan et al., 2015), HES4 is identified by our present study capable of combating EMT induction in a BEST4-dependent manner that is regulated at both transcriptional and translational levels.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing HES4's effects on EMT require BEST4, with citations to prior HES1 studies

claim: TWIST1 reprograms EMT by repressing the expression of E-cadherin and TJP1.
source: TWIST1 (a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor) reprograms EMT by repressing the expression of E-cadherin and TJP1 (Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004) and simultaneously inducing several mesenchymal markers, typically VIM (Bulzico et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004), which is a pivotal predictor of CRC progression (Vesuna et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2004; Yusup et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies

claim: TWIST1 simultaneously induces several mesenchymal markers, typically VIM.
source: TWIST1 (a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor) reprograms EMT by repressing the expression of E-cadherin and TJP1 (Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004) and simultaneously inducing several mesenchymal markers, typically VIM (Bulzico et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004), which is a pivotal predictor of CRC progression (Vesuna et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2004; Yusup et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies

claim: VIM is a pivotal predictor of CRC progression.
source: TWIST1 (a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor) reprograms EMT by repressing the expression of E-cadherin and TJP1 (Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004) and simultaneously inducing several mesenchymal markers, typically VIM (Bulzico et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2004), which is a pivotal predictor of CRC progression (Vesuna et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2004; Yusup et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies

claim: The HES4-BEST4-TWIST1 axis contributes to counter EMT in the development of CRC.
source: Although the mechanistic insights of their interplay remain to be elucidated, the present study identifies the HES4-BEST4-TWIST1 axis that contributes to counter EMT in the development of CRC (Figure 5G).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing interactions and effects on EMT markers, illustrated in Figure 5G

claim: The mRNA levels of BEST4 were lower in tissues of both precancerous adenomatous lesions and CRC than adjacent normal tissues.
source: In particular, the mRNA levels of BEST4 were lower in tissues of both precancerous adenomatous lesions and CRC than ANTs.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from patient samples

claim: Low BEST4 expression is significantly correlated with large tumour size, positive nodes, and poor overall survival.
source: These alterations are significantly correlated with large tumour size, positive nodes, and poor overall survival, especially in male patients.
evidence: Supported by clinicopathological correlation and survival analysis data

claim: There is an approximately 40% higher incidence of CRC in males than in females in a Chinese cohort.
source: Interestingly, a previous study conducted on a Chinese cohort reported an approximately 40% higher incidence of CRC in males than in females (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Zhang et al., 2019

claim: The study reveals a previously unknown mechanism of the HES4-BEST4-TWIST1 axis that restrains the progression of CRC.
source: Therefore, we reveals a previously unknown mechanism of the HES4-BEST4-TWIST1 axis that restrains the progression of CRC.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the collective findings of the study

claim: HES4 binds to the promoter region of BEST4.
source: Our findings support the notion in several ways: (1) HES4 binds to the promoter region of BEST4; (2) BEST4 colocalises with HES4 and TWIST1 in the nucleus of cells, and protein-protein interactions; (3) the BEST4 inhibitory role in EMT exhibits upregulation of epithelial TJP1 and E-cadherin, and downregulation of mesenchymal VIM and TWIST1 in CRC; and finally (4) low BEST4 mRNA levels were significantly correlated with malignant lesions and worse outcomes of CRC patients.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing HES4 binding to BEST4 promoter

claim: BEST4 colocalises with HES4 and TWIST1 in the nucleus of cells.
source: Our findings support the notion in several ways: (1) HES4 binds to the promoter region of BEST4; (2) BEST4 colocalises with HES4 and TWIST1 in the nucleus of cells, and protein-protein interactions; (3) the BEST4 inhibitory role in EMT exhibits upregulation of epithelial TJP1 and E-cadherin, and downregulation of mesenchymal VIM and TWIST1 in CRC; and finally (4) low BEST4 mRNA levels were significantly correlated with malignant lesions and worse outcomes of CRC patients.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data
